title: How '4 Easy Payments of $19' Hacks Your Brain's Pain Center
alt_title_1: The Neuroscience Trick Behind Buy Now, Pay Later
alt_title_2: Why Splitting Payments Increases Impulse Spending by 38%
description_hook: Stanford neuroeconomics research explains why '4 interest-free payments of $19' sedates the insula - your brain's natural spending brake - triggering up to 38% higher impulse spend. Here is the Full-Price Cash Rule to fight back.

scenes.headline: Why $19 x 4 Feels Cheaper Than $76
scenes.stat_label: CHECKOUT DESIGN THAT NUMBS YOUR SPENDING BRAKE
bullets: Zero-interest split buttons look mathematically free
Psychologically they rewire how you judge cost
scenes.narration: Splitting a seventy-six-dollar checkout into four easy payments of nineteen dollars looks harmless - until you see how it sedates your brain's alarm system.

scenes.headline: Stanford's 'Pain of Paying' Brain Scans
scenes.stat_label: BRAIN REGION THAT FIRES WHEN YOU SEE FULL PRICES
bullets: Upfront cash prices trigger healthy neural friction
That discomfort evolved to stop bad impulse trades
scenes.narration: Stanford brain-imaging studies found that seeing a full price tag activates the insula, the exact neural region that processes physical pain, acting as a natural brake on impulse buying.

scenes.headline: Payment Decoupling Multiplies Micro-Bills
scenes.left_body: Reward today, fragmented pain later -> +38% spend
scenes.right_body: Honest price signal today -> clean future paycheck
scenes.narration: Buy-now-pay-later buttons exploit payment decoupling. By shrinking seventy-six dollars into nineteen today, checkout screens numb that pain signal and push shoppers to spend up to thirty-eight percent more.

scenes.headline: The Full-Price Cash Clarity Rule
scenes.stat_subtext: Pay 100% upfront for non-essentials or close the tab
scenes.narration: Protect your margin with the Full-Price Cash Rule: never split a non-essential purchase into installments. If paying the full amount stings today, close the tab.
